q: 1. Dead storage in a reservoir is provided .............
options: to accommodated the silt trapped in the reservoir
to increase the useful life period
explain: Dead storage is the volume below the lowest outlet level; it is reserved for the accumulation of sediment (silt) over the dam's design life.

q: 2. Which of the following is a rigid dam?
explain: Gravity dams are rigid structures made of concrete or masonry that resist the forces of water through their own weight and structural stiffness.

q: 3. Arch dams are generally preferred in .............
options: wide rivers with good foundation at shallow depth
reservoirs where provision is made for future increase in capacity
explain: Arch dams transfer most of the water pressure to the side walls (abutments), requiring a narrow valley and very strong rock on both sides.

q: 4. The water is not suitable for irrigation if the total salt concentration exceeds .............
explain: High salinity (Total Dissolved Solids) creates osmotic pressure that makes it difficult for plants to absorb water. 2000 ppm is generally considered the upper limit for most crops.

q: 5. The water is unsuitable for irrigation when the boron content exceeds the limit of .............
explain: While boron is a necessary micronutrient, it is toxic to many plants even in small concentrations; 2 ppm is usually the threshold for 'unsuitable' classification.

q: 6. Which of the following is the aggrading river?
options: neither loosing nor building its bed
developing a high degree of sinuosity
explain: An aggrading river is one that collects sediment and debris, gradually raising its bed level over time due to an excess silt charge.

q: 7. Guide banks are provided .............
options: to train the flow of a river along a specified course
to confine the width of the river
explain: Guide banks (Bell's Bunds) are used near bridges or weirs to funnel the river flow smoothly through the structure and prevent it from outflanking the work.

q: 8. Spurs are provided .............
options: to train the flow of a river along a specified course
to confine the width of the river
explain: Spurs (or groynes) are structures built from the river bank toward the center to deflect the current away from the bank, protecting it from erosion.

q: 9. In a repelling groyne, the axis of the groyne (with respect to the river flow direction) makes .............
explain: A repelling groyne points upstream (obtuse angle with the downstream direction). This deflects the current toward the center of the river and creates a still water pocket u/s.

q: 10. In a deflecting groyne, the axis the groyne (with respect to the river flow direction) marks .............
explain: A deflecting groyne is built perpendicular (90°) to the bank. It simply deflects the current without specifically attracting or repelling the flow significantly.

q: 11. With age, the trap efficiency of a reservoir is likely to .............
explain: As a reservoir ages, it fills with silt, which reduces its capacity. Since the Capacity-Inflow ratio decreases, the trap efficiency also decreases.

q: 12. The type of dam recommended for a site with narrow gorge and steep and strong side slopes is .............
explain: Arch dams are structurally ideal for narrow canyons with strong rock walls (abutments) because they transfer the load through arch action to the canyon sides.

q: 13. The process of washing out of the salt from the upper zone of the soil by flooding is called .............
explain: Leaching is an agricultural technique where excess water is applied to the land to dissolve salts and carry them down into the subsoil or drainage system.

q: 14. At what fraction of depth below the free surface does the average velocity occur in open channel flow .............
explain: In practical hydraulics, the velocity measured at 0.6 of the depth from the surface is considered to be approximately equal to the mean (average) velocity of the vertical.

q: 15. An impervious wall inside an earthen dam to reduce the seepage is called .............
explain: These are all terms for the central impervious barrier (often made of clay or concrete) used in earth dams to control seepage through the body of the dam.

q: 16. An obstruction of small height built across a stream to divert water into an off take channel is known as .............
explain: A diversion headwork (like a weir or barrage) is designed primarily to raise the water level and divert it into a canal, rather than storing it.

q: 17. An earthen embankment built on each side of a river for some distance as a flood control measure is called .............
explain: Dykes (also called levees or marginal bunds) are constructed parallel to the river bank to contain floodwaters within the channel.

q: 18. The top of the capillary zone .............
options: lies above the piezometric surface at all points
lies below the piezometric surface at all points
explain: Capillary action pulls water upward against gravity from the water table (piezometric surface), so the top of the capillary zone is always higher than the actual water table.

q: 19. The vertical component of the hydrostatic force on an inclined surface is obtained as .............
options: as the weight of water resting on the inclined surface
explain: The vertical force on any submerged surface is equal to the weight of the volume of liquid vertically above that surface extending up to the free surface.

q: 20. The irrigation with sewage, (instead of natural water) where the disposal of sewage is the prime object is called .............
explain: Broad irrigation is the process of spreading raw or partially treated sewage over large areas of land to simultaneously treat the waste and grow crops.

q: 21. The difference in levels between the top of capillary zone and the water table is
explain: The capillary zone exists above the water table due to surface tension pulling water upward; therefore, its top level is higher (positive difference) than the water table level.

q: 22. Natural fertility is generally found in
explain: Alluvial soils, formed by river deposits, are rich in minerals and nutrients, making them naturally the most fertile soil type for agriculture.

q: 23. The critical hydraulic gradient, according to Khosla's theory, in alluvial soils is approximately
explain: The critical hydraulic gradient ($i_c$) at which soil particles begin to move (boiling) is roughly $(G-1)/(1+e)$, which for most alluvial soils is approximately 1.0.

q: 24. The irrigation is necessary in an area
options: where there is a scanty rainfall
where commercial crops require more water
explain: Irrigation acts as an artificial supplement to ensure crops receive sufficient moisture regardless of natural rainfall patterns or high-demand crop requirements.

q: 25. Which of the salt present in water is harmful for cultivation purposes?
explain: Sodium carbonate (Black Alkali) is highly harmful as it reacts with soil to form a hard, impermeable crust and significantly raises soil pH.

q: 26. The whole period of cultivation from the time when irrigation water is first supplied for preparation of the ground to its last watering before harvesting, is called
explain: Base period ($B$) is used in engineering calculations for duty and delta; it is slightly shorter than the crop period.

q: 27. For closed growing crops (such as wheat), the method of irrigation used is
explain: Border flooding is very effective for close-growing crops like wheat or barley because it provides uniform distribution over long strips.

q: 28. Check flooding method of irrigation is used for
options: crops which can stand inundation of water for sometime
crops such as sugarcane, potatoes etc.
explain: Check flooding involves surrounding plots with low levees; it is ideal for heavy soils or crops like rice that can handle standing water.

q: 29. The method of irrigation used for orchards is
explain: In basin flooding, a circular or square basin is formed around each tree or group of trees, which is common in orchard management.

q: 30. The precipitation caused by natural rising of warmer lighter air colder and denser surroundings is called
explain: Convective precipitation occurs when the earth's surface is heated, causing warm air to rise, cool, and condense into rain.

q: 31. Run-off is measure in
explain: Run-off rate (discharge) is conventionally measured in cubic meters per second (cumecs).

q: 32. Irrigation canals are generally aligned along
explain: Aligning along the watershed (ridge) is preferred because it eliminates the need for expensive cross-drainage works.

q: 33. The infertility of the soil in water-logged areas is due to
options: inhibiting activity of the soil bacteria
explain: Waterlogging leads to anaerobic conditions (killing aerobic bacteria), salt accumulation (salinization), and the proliferation of water-loving weeds.

q: 34. Water logging is caused due to
explain: It is generally caused by a combination of excessive water input (rain/irrigation) and the inability of that water to drain away naturally or artificially.

q: 35. The soil becomes, practically, infertile if its pH value is
explain: A pH of 11 indicates highly alkaline (sodic) soil, which is toxic to most crops and destroys soil structure.

q: 36. A river meandering through an alluvial plain has a series of consecutive reversed order connected with short straight sketches, is called .............
explain: A 'crossing' is the relatively short, straight reach of a river between two consecutive reverse bends (meanders).

q: 37. When river flows in a plain country, its stage is known as ............. stage.
explain: The 'trough' or 'alluvial' stage occurs when the river reaches the plains, characterized by a bed of sand and silt rather than boulders.

q: 38. The method used for training of rivers is .............
explain: River training involves various structures: Guide banks (flow direction), Levees (flood protection), and Groynes (bank protection/channel narrowing).

q: 39. A deflecting groyne has a much ............. length than a repelling groyne.
explain: Deflecting groynes are short and only change the local flow direction, whereas repelling groynes are longer and designed to push the main current away.

q: 40. A deflecting groyne in a river is .............
explain: Deflecting groynes are typically inclined downstream (pointing with the flow) to nudge the current away from the bank.

q: 41. A levee on flood .............
options: increases the water surface elevation of the river at flood
decreases the surface slope of the stream above the leveed portion
increases the velocity and scouring action through leveed section
explain: Levees confine floodwaters, which naturally raises the water level, increases velocity due to lack of lateral spread, and changes the energy gradient.

q: 42. A groyne with a curved head is known as .............
explain: A Burma-type groyne is specifically characterized by having a curved or T-shaped head to provide better flow stabilization at the tip.

q: 43. The measure to remove water logging of land, is .............
options: to increase outflow from the ground water reservoir
explain: Remediation involves both prevention (lining canals to stop seepage) and drainage (pumping or surface drains to lower the water table).

q: 44. The water face of the guide banks, is protected by .............
explain: The term 'one-man stone' refers to stones that can be handled by one person, commonly used for pitching guide banks to prevent erosion.

q: 45. Attracting groynes are built .............
explain: Attracting groynes point downstream; this orientation 'invites' the current toward the bank they are attached to, usually to move the channel away from the opposite bank.
